extracted.intended_audience: U.S. patent examiners and patent practitioners (applicants/attorneys)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for determining when 35 U.S.C. 112(f) (pre-AIA 112 sixth paragraph) applies to claim limitations and what disclosure and linking of corresponding structure/material/acts (including computer-implemented algorithms) is required in the specification to avoid indefiniteness and satisfy written description/enablement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption that 'means' or generic placeholders invoke 35 U.S.C. 112(f)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners will apply 35 U.S.C. 112(f) to a claim limitation that uses the term 'means' or generic placeholder associated with functional language, unless that term is (1) preceded by a structural modifier, defined in the specification as a particular structure or known by one skilled in the art, that denotes the type of structural device (e.g., 'filters'), or (2) otherwise modified by sufficient structure or the claimed function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also applies analogously to 'step for' unless modified by sufficient acts. Applicant may rebut this presumption by adding sufficient structure/material/acts in the claim; the USPTO will consider the presumption rebutted until such modifying language is deleted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural modifier avoids 112(f) treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: A limitation will not invoke 35 U.S.C. 112(f) if there is a structural modifier that further describes the term 'means' or the generic placeholder (e.g., 'detent mechanism' did not invoke 112(f) because 'detent' denotes a type of structural device with a generally understood meaning in the mechanical arts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By contrast, a generic placeholder coupled with a function may invoke 112(f) when preceded by a non-structural modifier that has no generally understood structural meaning in the art (e.g., 'colorant selection mechanism', 'movable link member').

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-prong check for whether coupled term denotes structure
rubrics_metrics.description: To determine whether a word, term, or phrase coupled with a function denotes structure, examiners may check whether: (1) the specification provides a description sufficient to inform one of ordinary skill in the art that the term denotes structure; (2) general and subject matter specific dictionaries provide evidence the term is recognized as a noun denoting structure; and/or (3) the prior art provides evidence the term is an art-recognized structure to perform the claimed function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Ex parte Rodriguez (precedential). Use these sources to decide whether the term conveys structural meaning to a POSITA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Element-by-element determination of 112(f) applicability
rubrics_metrics.description: It is necessary to decide on an element by element basis whether 35 U.S.C. 112(f) applies. Each claim must be independently reviewed to determine the applicability of 35 U.S.C. 112(f) even where the application contains substantially similar process and apparatus claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims should not be interpreted as means- or step-plus-function solely because other claims use that form; interpret each limitation in context of the claim language and specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corresponding structure must be disclosed in the specification
rubrics_metrics.description: The corresponding structure (or material or acts) of a means- (or step-) plus-function limitation must be disclosed in the specification itself in a way that one skilled in the art will understand what structure (or material or acts) will perform the recited function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If no disclosure of structure/material/acts exists, the claim fails 35 U.S.C. 112(b). The disclosure may be implicit or inherent if clear to those skilled in the art; however, a bare statement that known techniques can be used does not disclose structure (Biomedino).

rubrics_metrics.name: Written description/enablement requirements still apply
rubrics_metrics.description: Invocation of 35 U.S.C. 112(f) does not exempt an applicant from compliance with 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (written description/enablement) and 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (definiteness) (or pre-AIA corresponding paragraphs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Means-plus-function language can be used but claims must still accurately define the invention and the specification must adequately disclose sufficient structure. Use In re Donaldson, In re Knowlton, Atmel, and related cases as guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drawings and implicit disclosure may support corresponding structure in limited circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: Under certain limited circumstances, drawings may provide a written description of corresponding structure, and disclosure of structure may be implicit/inherent if it would have been clear to those skilled in the art what structure must perform the function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Dossel and Vas-Cath. But implicit statements like 'may be controlled by known techniques' are insufficient (Biomedino).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambiguous or inconclusive 3-prong analysis leads to examiner determination and applicant opportunity
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim may be indefinite when the 3-prong analysis for determining whether the limitation should be interpreted under 112(f) is inconclusive because of ambiguous words in the claim. Examiner should determine whether the words recite sufficiently definite structure; applicant can present arguments or amend claims to clarify whether 112(f) applies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner must consider claim language, specification, and how a POSITA would understand the language in light of disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computer-implemented 112(f) limitations require disclosure of an algorithm
rubrics_metrics.description: For a computer-implemented 35 U.S.C. 112(f) claim limitation, the specification must disclose an algorithm for performing the claimed specific computer function, or else the claim is indefinite under 35 U.S.C. 112(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The disclosed structure is the special purpose computer programmed to perform the disclosed algorithm (not merely a general purpose computer). See NetMoneyIN, Aoyama, WMS, Aristocrat, Noah Systems and related cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: General purpose computer alone is usually insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: A general purpose computer or microprocessor can serve as structure only where the claimed function is 'coextensive' with a microprocessor itself (rare circumstances such as 'receiving', 'storing', 'processing'). All other computer-implemented functions require disclosure of an algorithm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EON Corp., Katz, Ergo Licensing. If only a general purpose computer is disclosed without special programming/algorithm, treat as pure functional claiming and likely indefinite.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algorithm sufficiency judged by POSITA skill level; acceptable forms of algorithm disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: An algorithm is a finite sequence of steps for solving a logical or mathematical problem or performing a task. Applicant may express the algorithm in any understandable terms including as a mathematical formula, in prose, in a flow chart, or 'in any other manner that provides sufficient structure.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adequacy is determined in view of what one of ordinary skill in the art would understand as sufficient to define the structure and make claim boundaries understandable. See Finisar, Intel, In re Dossel, Typhoon Touch.

rubrics_metrics.name: When multiple functions are recited, specification must disclose structure/algorithm for all functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a means-plus-function limitation performs multiple identifiable functions, the specification must disclose adequate corresponding structure (algorithm) to perform all of the claimed functions; disclosure that covers only some functions is treated as if no algorithm was disclosed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Williamson, Noah, Media Rights and related cases: failure to disclose an algorithm for one of multiple functions renders the limitation indefinite.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere references to 'software', 'logic', or black-box components are insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Mere reference to a general purpose computer with appropriate programming, or simply reciting 'software' without providing detail about how to accomplish a specific software function, or referencing an undefined component (e.g., 'access control manager'), 'logic', or 'code' (black box), is not an adequate disclosure of corresponding structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There must be some explanation of how the computer or computer component performs the claimed function; see Blackboard, NetMoneyIN, Finisar.

rubrics_metrics.name: Means-plus-function limitation limits claim to disclosed implementation mode (hardware/software) and equivalents
rubrics_metrics.description: By choosing to use a means-plus-function limitation and invoke 35 U.S.C. 112(f), applicant limits that claim limitation to the disclosed structure, i.e., implementation by hardware or the combination of hardware and software, and equivalents thereof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner should not construe the limitation as covering pure software implementation if the disclosure points to hardware or hardware/software combination. If only software is disclosed without algorithm, the limitation is indefinite.

rubrics_metrics.name: If unclear whether supporting structure or algorithm is adequate, appropriate rejection is under 112(b)
rubrics_metrics.description: If it is unclear whether there is sufficient supporting structure or whether the algorithm is adequate to perform the entire claimed function, it is appropriate to reject the claim under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (or pre-AIA 112 second paragraph).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When rejected as indefinite for lacking corresponding structure/algorithm, the claim will also likely lack written description under 112(a); examiner should consider enablement and written description MPEP sections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insufficiency of specification disclosure results in failure of 112(b) and written description
rubrics_metrics.description: If there is no disclosure of structure, material or acts for performing the recited function, the claim fails to satisfy the requirements of 35 U.S.C. 112(b). Such insufficiency is closely related to failure to satisfy the written description (35 U.S.C. 112(a)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited cases: Atmel, Biomedino, Budde, Cardiac Pacemakers, Aristocrat, In re Noll. Examiner should assess whether specification demonstrates possession and enables the full scope of claimed invention (see MPEP §§2161.01, 2163.03, 2164.08).
